questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: A crocodilian exception prevents four heart chambers from being used as a unique class marker
questions.syllabus_anchor: Animal kingdom: chordates; salient features and classification of vertebrates
questions.question: Three vertebrates are compared. P has a three-chambered heart, moist glandular skin and a larval stage with gills; Q has dry scales, a four-chambered heart and lays shelled eggs on land; R has feathers and a four-chambered heart. Which classification uses the combination of traits without treating heart-chamber number as sufficient?
options: A) P Reptilia; Q Aves; R Amphibia
B) P Amphibia; Q Aves; R Reptilia
C) P Amphibia; Q Reptilia, represented by a crocodilian; R Aves
D) P Pisces; Q Mammalia; R Aves
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) P is an amphibian, Q a crocodilian reptile and R a bird.
Why: P combines the moist glandular covering and aquatic larval respiration characteristic of amphibians. Most reptiles have an incompletely divided ventricle, but crocodilians have a four-chambered heart; dry scales and shelled terrestrial eggs place Q with reptiles despite this exception. Feathers identify R as a bird. Thus the same heart-chamber count can occur in different vertebrate classes, and several independent characters must be combined.
Why not the others: (A) exchanges the amphibian and reptile coverings and ignores R's feathers. (B) assigns a featherless scaled animal to birds and a feathered animal to reptiles. (D) gills in an amphibian larva do not make the adult a fish, and Q lacks the diagnostic mammalian combination.
Key point: Classify using a coherent character set while retaining genuine exceptions to broad generalisations.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.topic: Structural Organisation In Plants And Animals
questions.sub_topic: Guard-cell specialisation and alternative stomatal geometry distinguished from ordinary epidermal cells
questions.syllabus_anchor: Anatomy of flowering plants: epidermal tissue system; stomata and guard cells
questions.question: The diagram compares two mature epidermal stomatal complexes. P has kidney-shaped guard cells and Q has dumbbell-shaped guard cells; the surrounding epidermal cells lack the dark chloroplast bodies shown in the guard cells. Which interpretation is supported?
options: A) Both regulate a pore, although guard-cell geometry differs; chloroplast absence in ordinary epidermal cells does not imply absence from guard cells
B) Only P is a stoma because all guard cells must be kidney-shaped
C) The dark bodies establish that every epidermal cell is photosynthetic
D) Q must be a xylem vessel because its guard cells are elongated
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Different guard-cell shapes can operate the same stomatal function.
Why: Each complex consists of a pore bounded by two specialised guard cells. Kidney-shaped guard cells occur widely, whereas the dumbbell form is characteristic of grasses. Guard cells can contain chloroplasts even when the ordinary epidermal cells shown lack them. The diagram therefore compares specialisation within the epidermis rather than two different vascular tissues. It does not establish a photosynthetic function for every surrounding cell.
Why not the others: (B) incorrectly makes one common guard-cell shape universal. (C) transfers a feature of the specialised guard cells to all epidermal cells despite the observed contrast. (D) confuses a paired surface pore apparatus with an internal conducting vessel.
Key point: Identify a tissue component by its organisation and role, allowing specialised cells to differ from their neighbours.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Saturating initial rates scale with active-site number without changing the half-maximum substrate concentration
questions.syllabus_anchor: Biomolecules: enzymes; factors affecting enzyme activity; substrate concentration
questions.question: Two identical enzyme preparations are assayed at the same optimal pH and temperature with saturating substrate. Preparation Q contains twice as much active enzyme as P. Initial rates are measured before appreciable substrate depletion. Which pair of changes is expected for Q relative to P?
options: A) Maximum rate unchanged; substrate concentration needed for half-maximum rate doubled
B) Maximum rate halved; half-maximum substrate concentration unchanged
C) Both maximum rate and half-maximum substrate concentration doubled
D) Maximum rate doubled; half-maximum substrate concentration unchanged
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Doubling active enzyme doubles maximum rate without changing the substrate dependence of each active site.
Why: With substrate saturating, the number of functioning catalytic sites limits the initial total rate. Q has twice as many equivalent sites, so it can process twice as much substrate per unit time. The molecular affinity and turnover properties of each enzyme molecule are unchanged under the matched conditions. Therefore the substrate concentration giving half of that preparation's own maximum remains the same. The initial-rate condition prevents later substrate depletion from obscuring this comparison.
Why not the others: (A) keeps the site-limited maximum fixed and wrongly changes the enzyme's substrate dependence. (B) reverses the effect of adding active catalytic sites. (C) confuses a vertical rate scaling with a change in the horizontal substrate-concentration scale.
Key point: Separate enzyme abundance from the properties of an individual catalytic site.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Division competence determines arithmetic versus geometric cell-lineage growth
questions.syllabus_anchor: Plant growth and development: arithmetic and geometric growth; differentiation
questions.question: A model plant cell lineage starts with one dividing cell. In lineage P each division produces one cell that keeps dividing and one cell that permanently differentiates. In lineage Q both daughters keep dividing. Cells divide once per equal interval, with no death. After four intervals, what are the total cell counts P and Q, and the corresponding growth patterns?
options: A) P=4, Q=8; both arithmetic
B) P=5, Q=16; arithmetic and geometric respectively
C) P=8, Q=16; geometric and arithmetic respectively
D) P=16, Q=5; geometric and arithmetic respectively
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) P contains 5 cells and Q 16 cells; their increments follow arithmetic and geometric growth respectively.
Given: Each lineage begins with one cell and undergoes four equal division intervals without loss.
Formula/Principle: Count only daughters retaining division competence when determining the next interval's increase.
Step 1: P always has one dividing cell. Each interval adds one differentiated cell, so \[N_P=1+4=5.\]
Step 2: Every Q cell divides, giving \[N_Q=1\times2^4=16.\]
Why: P's constant dividing compartment produces a constant absolute increase, whereas Q's expanding dividing compartment produces a constant proportional increase. Differentiated daughters remain in the total count but do not generate further descendants in this model.
Why not the others: (A) omits the initial cell and undercounts Q's doubling. (C) gives P geometric proliferation contrary to permanent differentiation. (D) exchanges the two lineage rules.
Key point: Growth depends on which descendants remain able to divide, not just the occurrence of mitosis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: An early spike can use existing ion gradients despite inhibition of their long-term pump maintenance
questions.syllabus_anchor: Neural control and coordination: generation and conduction of nerve impulse
questions.question: An isolated axon initially has normal ion gradients. A brief treatment blocks the sodium–potassium pump but does not block voltage-gated channels. Before the gradients substantially dissipate, a threshold stimulus is applied. Which statement best separates the action potential from long-term gradient maintenance?
options: A) An initial action potential can still occur through channel-mediated ion movement, although prolonged pump inhibition will impair maintenance of the gradients
B) The pump must carry the inward sodium current of every depolarising spike
C) Potassium must enter the axon through the pump to generate the rapid repolarising current
D) Blocking the pump immediately makes both sides of the membrane have identical ion concentrations
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Existing gradients can support an initial channel-mediated spike despite loss of their active maintenance.
Why: Rapid depolarisation normally involves increased sodium permeability through gated channels, followed by increased potassium permeability during repolarisation. These passive movements use electrochemical gradients already present before the stimulus. The sodium–potassium pump supports those gradients over longer periods but is not the gated pathway carrying each rapid spike current. The stipulated short observation interval matters: after extended inhibition, repeated activity and ion leakage would undermine the gradients and excitability.
Why not the others: (B) replaces the voltage-gated sodium pathway with the slower maintenance pump. (C) reverses the usual outward potassium movement during repolarisation and assigns it to the wrong mechanism. (D) assumes inhibition instantly removes previously established concentration differences.
Key point: Distinguish the pathway producing an electrical event from the process maintaining its energy source.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Preventing ovulation does not supply a barrier against sexually transmitted infection
questions.syllabus_anchor: Reproductive health: contraception; sexually transmitted infections and prevention
questions.question: A couple correctly uses oral contraceptive pills. They believe this also protects them from sexually transmitted infections. Which advice correctly distinguishes contraceptive action from infection prevention?
options: A) Hormonal suppression of ovulation necessarily prevents entry of HIV
B) An intrauterine device should replace the pill because it reliably blocks all sexually transmitted pathogens
C) Continue suitable contraception if desired, but use condoms to reduce sexual transmission risk; hormonal contraception alone does not provide that barrier
D) Condoms prevent infection only when ovulation is simultaneously suppressed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Hormonal contraception and a physical barrier address different routes to different outcomes.
Why: Oral contraceptives alter reproductive hormonal control and can prevent ovulation or otherwise reduce pregnancy probability. That action does not prevent contact with infectious secretions or pathogens during sexual intercourse. Correct condom use provides a barrier that reduces transmission risk as well as contributing to contraception. Risk reduction should not be described as an absolute guarantee, and neither pill use nor an intrauterine device substitutes for the relevant barrier.
Why not the others: (A) confuses blocking egg release with blocking pathogen entry. (B) incorrectly attributes universal infection protection to an intrauterine device. (D) makes a barrier's infection-prevention role depend on the ovarian cycle, although pathogen exposure does not require ovulation.
Key point: Evaluate pregnancy prevention and infection-risk reduction as separate biological mechanisms.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Bird ZW, human XY and honeybee haplodiploidy differ in the variable parental contribution
questions.syllabus_anchor: Principles of inheritance and variation: sex determination in humans, birds and honeybees
questions.question: Ignore exceptional sex-determination mechanisms. A hen produces Z-bearing or W-bearing eggs; a human female produces X-bearing eggs; a queen honeybee can lay fertilised or unfertilised eggs. Which comparison is correct?
options: A) The male determines chromosomal sex in all three systems
B) Only the female's egg type matters in both birds and humans
C) An unfertilised honeybee egg develops into a diploid female
D) The egg's Z/W contribution determines bird sex, the sperm's X/Y contribution determines human sex, and fertilisation normally distinguishes diploid female from haploid male honeybees
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The variable parental contribution differs among the three systems.
Why: Female birds are ZW and males ZZ, so alternative eggs provide the variable sex chromosome. In humans the female is XX and the male XY, making sperm type the variable chromosomal contribution. In honeybees, ordinary unfertilised eggs develop parthenogenetically into haploid males, whereas fertilised eggs develop into diploid females. These mechanisms cannot be collapsed into one universal rule about which parent determines sex.
Why not the others: (A) wrongly applies the human XY pattern to birds and haplodiploidy. (B) ignores the human male's alternative X- and Y-bearing sperm. (C) reverses both the ploidy and the usual sex of an unfertilised honeybee egg.
Key point: Identify the heterogametic parent or fertilisation rule before assigning a parental sex-determining role.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Controlled allergen evidence, self-antigen injury and helper-cell deficiency distinguish three immune failures
questions.syllabus_anchor: Human health and disease: allergy; autoimmunity; immunodeficiency
questions.question: Three patients are investigated. P develops a rapid wheal after a harmless pollen challenge; a matched test without pollen is negative and allergen-specific IgE is elevated. Q has antibodies reacting with the patient's own joint tissue and inflammatory injury. R repeatedly develops opportunistic infections and has severely reduced helper T-cell counts. Which assignment fits the targets and response evidence?
options: A) P autoimmunity; Q allergy; R enhanced innate defence
B) P allergy; Q autoimmunity; R immune deficiency
C) P immune deficiency; Q allergy; R autoimmunity
D) All three are explained by antibodies attacking pollen
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) P shows allergy, Q autoimmunity and R immune deficiency.
Why: P has an antigen-dependent excessive response to an ordinarily harmless environmental substance, consistent with an IgE-associated allergy. Q's response is directed against self tissue, which identifies loss of self tolerance rather than an exaggerated response to an external allergen. R has impaired helper T-cell availability together with infections that normally controlled immunity would resist. The matched negative challenge in P separates the observed pollen response from an unrelated skin reaction; the three cases therefore require both the target and the effectiveness of defence to be considered.
Why not the others: (A) exchanges the external and self targets and misreads reduced defence as enhancement. (C) reverses the evidence for P and R and assigns Q the wrong target class. (D) ignores the distinct self-directed response and T-cell deficit.
Key point: Distinguish excessive external-antigen responses, self-directed responses and insufficient protective responses.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Host barriers determine competence treatment, microinjection or biolistic DNA delivery
questions.syllabus_anchor: Biotechnology principles and processes: methods of introducing recombinant DNA into host cells
questions.question: Three DNA-delivery tasks are planned: P introduces DNA into chemically treated bacterial cells; Q delivers DNA directly into the nucleus of an animal cell; R delivers DNA across a plant cell wall without first making protoplasts. Which methods match these physical barriers?
options: A) P microinjection; Q biolistics; R heat-shock transformation
B) P biolistics; Q chemical competence; R microinjection into a bacterial nucleus
C) P competence treatment followed by heat shock; Q microinjection; R DNA-coated particle bombardment
D) P chemical competence; Q heat shock only; R removal of all plant walls by the gene gun
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The methods act on different barriers and target compartments.
Why: Chemical competence treatment can increase bacterial DNA uptake, with the appropriate heat-shock step aiding transformation. A fine micropipette can place DNA directly into an animal-cell nucleus during microinjection. Biolistics uses DNA-coated particles to cross plant-cell barriers, including walls, and does not require every target cell to be converted into a protoplast first. Successful delivery still does not by itself prove stable integration or expression.
Why not the others: (A) swaps direct animal-cell injection with plant particle delivery and gives the intact plant the bacterial procedure. (B) invokes a bacterial nucleus, which bacteria lack, and mismatches the targets. (D) wrongly treats heat shock as precise nuclear injection and claims a gene gun removes all walls.
Key point: Choose a delivery method from the cell barrier and intended destination before judging genetic success.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Biomass, numerical density and percentage cover answer different population questions
questions.syllabus_anchor: Organisms and populations: population density and its alternative measures
questions.question: A lake contains a few very large fish and thousands of tiny plankton, while a rock face carries a spreading lichen mat whose individuals cannot be separated reliably. Which measurements best answer respectively: fish contribution to living mass, plankton abundance, and extent of lichen occupation?
options: A) Fish biomass; plankton number per volume; lichen percentage cover
B) Fish number alone; plankton average length alone; lichen number of disputed individuals
C) Fish occupied surface area; plankton colour; lichen water content
D) Use individual count alone in all three cases, because population density can never use biomass or cover
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Density can be expressed using the measure relevant to the organism and ecological question.
Why: Individual number can greatly understate the mass contribution of a few large organisms, so fish biomass addresses the first question directly. A standard-volume count gives a reproducible abundance measure for dispersed plankton. Percentage cover measures occupation by a lichen mat when boundaries between individuals are not operationally reliable. These measures are not interchangeable numerical units, but each can represent population presence or density for its specified purpose.
Why not the others: (B) supplies measurements that fail the mass, abundance or boundary constraints. (C) substitutes unrelated attributes for the requested quantities. (D) makes individual count universal despite the explicit difficulty of delimiting lichen individuals.
Key point: Define the biological quantity and sampling unit before choosing a density measure.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: ABO offspring possibilities separate codominance within an individual from multiple alleles in a population
questions.syllabus_anchor: Principles of inheritance and variation: multiple alleles; ABO blood groups; codominance
questions.question: Two parents with blood group AB have a child. Assume the usual ABO alleles and no rare phenotypes. Which statement correctly links the possible child phenotypes to the meaning of multiple alleles and codominance?
options: A) Their child can be O because AB parents transmit the recessive allele i
B) Every child must be AB because the parental alleles blend permanently
C) Each parent contains all three alleles IA, IB and i in the same diploid locus
D) A, AB and B children are possible; IA and IB are codominant in an AB individual, while the population contains more than two alleles at the locus
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The cross permits A, AB and B, and illustrates two distinct genetic terms.
Why: Each AB parent transmits either IA or IB. Their offspring can therefore be IAIA, IAIB or IBIB, producing A, AB or B phenotypes. IA and IB are both expressed in a heterozygous AB individual, which is codominance. Multiple allelism instead describes the existence of IA, IB and i in the population; one ordinary diploid individual still carries only two alleles at the locus. Neither parent in this cross carries i.
Why not the others: (A) invents an i allele absent from both parental genotypes. (B) treats codominance as permanent blending that abolishes segregation. (C) confuses the population's allele inventory with an individual's diploid genotype.
Key point: Separate allele transmission, heterozygous expression and population-level allele diversity.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Observed linkage strength does not uniquely determine a ratio of physical chromosome distances
questions.syllabus_anchor: Principles of inheritance and variation: linkage and recombination
questions.question: In the same species, two separate linked marker pairs P–Q and R–S give recombinant fractions of 0.10 and 0.45 in large test crosses, with no viability differences. Which inference is justified without additional physical or multi-marker data?
options: A) R–S must occupy different chromosomes because their recombinant fraction exceeds 0.25
B) P–Q show stronger observed linkage; the 0.45 value does not establish that the physical distance is exactly 4.5 times as large
C) P–Q must be physically farther apart because fewer recombinants survived
D) The physical distance of either pair is fixed uniquely by its recombinant fraction even if multiple crossovers occur
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Recombinant fractions compare observed linkage but do not uniquely measure long physical distances.
Why: Fewer recombinant offspring indicate stronger observed association for P–Q under the stated equal-viability conditions. A fraction close to one-half can arise from widely separated loci on the same chromosome as well as independent assortment, so R–S need not lie on different chromosomes. Multiple exchanges can restore parental marker arrangements and go uncounted as recombinants. Therefore the two fractions cannot be converted into an exact ratio of DNA lengths using these data alone.
Why not the others: (A) invents a 0.25 boundary for different chromosomes. (C) contradicts both the linkage interpretation and the exclusion of differential survival. (D) ignores undetected multiple exchanges and variation in recombination along chromosomes.
Key point: Recombination is evidence for association, not an unlimited ruler for physical DNA distance.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: ECG ventricular depolarisation precedes pressure-driven valve opening and actual ejection
questions.syllabus_anchor: Body fluids and circulation: ECG; cardiac cycle; pressure-dependent valve function
questions.question: The aligned trace shows a normal ECG and left-ventricular and aortic pressures. At marker X the QRS complex has just occurred, ventricular pressure is rising above left-atrial pressure but remains below aortic pressure. At Y the ventricular pressure first exceeds aortic pressure. Which sequence is consistent with excitation and valve mechanics?
options: A) X marks ventricular repolarisation and immediate semilunar opening; Y marks atrial depolarisation
B) The QRS complex is blood ejection itself, so the aortic valve must already be open at X
C) Ventricular depolarisation precedes pressure development; X can be isovolumetric contraction with both left-heart valves shut, and ejection begins near Y
D) The mitral valve stays open throughout X to Y because ventricular pressure is increasing
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Electrical excitation precedes force and the pressure crossing that opens the outlet valve.
Why: QRS reflects ventricular depolarisation, not the volume of blood being ejected. As contraction develops, ventricular pressure closes the mitral valve once it exceeds atrial pressure. Until it also exceeds aortic pressure, the aortic valve remains closed, so the intervening contraction can occur with both valves shut and no ejection. The crossing near Y supplies the pressure condition for aortic opening and the start of ejection. This combines the ECG with the pressure evidence instead of treating them as identical events.
Why not the others: (A) confuses depolarisation with repolarisation and opens the outlet too early. (B) equates an electrical waveform with a mechanical flow event. (D) contradicts the reversed pressure difference across the mitral valve at X.
Key point: Relate electrical activation to subsequent mechanics through pressure differences, not by equating ECG peaks with blood flow.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Peripheral doublets with a central pair distinguished from a nine-triplet basal-body cylinder
questions.syllabus_anchor: Cell the unit of life: cilia, flagella, centrosome and centrioles
questions.question: Two transverse microtubule schematics are shown. P has nine peripheral doublets and a central pair; Q has nine peripheral triplets and no central pair. Which interpretation correctly relates these organisations?
options: A) P is a typical eukaryotic ciliary or flagellar axoneme; Q is a centriole or basal-body pattern
B) P is a bacterial flagellum; Q is the 9+2 axoneme of a eukaryotic cilium
C) Both are identical because the number of peripheral groups is nine
D) P must contain 27 peripheral microtubules and Q only 18
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The doublet-plus-central-pair pattern differs from the triplet cylinder.
Why: The typical motile eukaryotic ciliary or flagellar axoneme has nine peripheral microtubule doublets and two central microtubules. Centrioles and basal bodies instead have nine peripheral triplets without that central pair. Nine peripheral groups alone therefore does not make the organisations identical. Bacterial flagella have a different protein organisation and are not built as the pictured 9+2 microtubule axoneme.
Why not the others: (B) exchanges the eukaryotic structures and incorrectly assigns microtubule architecture to a bacterial flagellum. (C) ignores doublet versus triplet membership and the centre. (D) reverses the peripheral totals: nine doublets contain 18 and nine triplets 27 microtubules.
Key point: Count both the peripheral group size and the central arrangement when identifying a microtubular structure.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Grazing and detritus pathways share producer-derived energy without cyclic energy regeneration
questions.syllabus_anchor: Ecosystem: energy flow; grazing and detritus food chains
questions.question: A forest's dead leaves enter a detritus food chain, while some living leaves are eaten by grazing herbivores. Which statement correctly describes the relation between the two routes and the energy source?
options: A) The detritus route creates new solar energy, so it needs no earlier producers
B) Energy consumed by decomposers is completely recycled back into sunlight
C) Only living-leaf feeding can transfer energy to consumers
D) Both routes can transfer energy originally fixed by producers; matter can recycle, but energy is progressively dissipated rather than regenerated in a closed biological cycle
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Grazing and detritus routes share producer-fixed energy without creating a cyclic energy supply.
Why: A living leaf and its later litter both contain chemical energy derived from primary production. Herbivores can receive some through grazing, whereas decomposers and detritivores can receive some after material enters the detritus pathway. Transfers involve respiration and heat dissipation, so the energy flow requires continuing external input. Recycling mineral nutrients does not restore dissipated energy to its original high-quality form.
Why not the others: (A) mistakes use of stored chemical energy for creation of new energy. (B) turns nutrient cycling into complete energy recycling. (C) denies the energy available to consumers of dead organic material.
Key point: Distinguish branching food pathways and matter recycling from the one-way degradation of usable energy.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: C2 molecular-orbital filling separates bond order from an assumed occupied 2p sigma bond
questions.syllabus_anchor: Chemical bonding: molecular orbital theory; homonuclear diatomic molecules
questions.question: For ground-state C2, use the valence molecular-orbital order shown: sigma(2s), sigma*(2s), pi(2px)=pi(2py), sigma(2pz). The bond axis is z. Fill eight valence electrons according to the usual rules. Which statement follows within this MO model?
options: A) Bond order 2, diamagnetic, with the occupied 2p bonding contribution entirely from the two pi orbitals
B) Bond order 2, paramagnetic, with two unpaired 2p electrons
C) Bond order 1, diamagnetic, because every filled 2p orbital is antibonding
D) Bond order 3, diamagnetic, with a filled sigma(2pz) orbital
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The stated ordering gives a diamagnetic bond-order-two configuration without occupied sigma(2pz).
Given: C2 supplies eight valence electrons and the diagram states the applicable orbital ordering.
Formula/Principle: Bond order is half the excess of bonding over antibonding electrons; unpaired occupancy determines magnetism.
Step 1: Four electrons fill sigma(2s) and sigma*(2s), whose bond-order contributions cancel.
Step 2: The remaining four occupy the two equal-energy pi bonding orbitals as paired electrons. Sigma(2pz) remains empty.
Step 3: \[\text{bond order}=(6-2)/2=2.\]
Why: This molecular-orbital description counts occupation of delocalised bonding and antibonding orbitals. It need not reproduce the simple localised rule that a drawn double bond is described as one sigma and one pi bond. Every occupied orbital here is paired.
Why not the others: (B) stops after single occupation instead of placing all four remaining electrons. (C) misidentifies the shown pi bonding levels as antibonding. (D) places electrons in a higher empty level without enough electrons.
Key point: Fill the stated MO ordering before importing a localised bond picture.
